desc:
A bag has n different kinds of tickets, and a draw takes a uniformly random kind each time (the drawn ticket goes back, so kinds can repeat). Let E be the expected number of draws until at least k different kinds have been seen.

E is a fraction p / q in lowest terms. Return p * q-1 modulo 1,000,000,007, that is, the residue that p / q stands for in modular arithmetic.

n = 2, k = 2 -> 3          (E = 2/2 + 2/1 = 3)
n = 3, k = 3 -> 500000009  (E = 11/2, and 2 * 500000009 = 11 mod p)
n = 4, k = 1 -> 1
hints: Once i kinds have been seen, each new draw is a new kind with probability (n - i) / n. How many draws does it take, on average, to see the next new kind?
The expected wait for a new kind from state i is n / (n - i). Expectations of consecutive stages add up, so sum over i = 0 .. k - 1.
Build the modular inverses of 1 .. n with the linear recurrence inv[i] = -(MOD // i) * inv[MOD % i] rather than calling pow for each term.
editorial: Count the draws in stages. Stage i starts when i different kinds have been seen and ends when the next new kind appears. In that stage each draw succeeds with probability (n - i) / n, so the number of draws in the stage is geometric with mean n / (n - i). The expected total is the sum of these means for i = 0 .. k - 1, which is E = sum n / (n - i) by linearity of expectation.

All denominators n - i are between 1 and n, far below the prime 1,000,000,007, so each one has a modular inverse. Computing the inverses one by one with fast exponentiation would cost O(n log MOD). A single linear pass that fills an inverse table costs O(n) and is also short to write.
The brute-force check solves the same process as a Markov chain with exact fractions: a backward recurrence on the number of kinds seen, which avoids the closed form entirely.
